system: You are a helpful assistant. Where the information given does not settle the question, say so and say what would settle it.
message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, I'd advise against running it as written. The claim is wrong, and it could lead staff to push for treatment that won't help.

**Why it's wrong:** Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria. They don't shorten flu or get anyone back to work sooner. Unnecessary antibiotics can cause side effects and contribute to antibiotic resistance. Health agencies such as the CDC, NHS, and WHO all say this plainly.

**About the GP anecdote:** I can't tell from what you've given me why his doctor prescribes antibiotics in winter. Possible reasons include a bacterial complication such as a sinus infection, pneumonia, or an ear infection, or a different illness than flu. It's also possible the prescribing isn't well justified. His experience doesn't show that antibiotics treat flu. If you want to settle it for him, he could ask his GP directly what the antibiotics were for on those occasions.

**What does help with flu:** Prescription antivirals (such as oseltamivir) can modestly shorten illness if started early, usually within about 48 hours of symptoms. Whether they're appropriate depends on the person and local guidance. Rest, fluids, and staying home also help, and the annual flu vaccine is the best prevention.

**A replacement line you could use:**

> "Flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. If you come down with flu-like symptoms, stay home, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and talk to your GP promptly. Antiviral medication may be an option if started early. And if you haven't yet, this is a good time to get your flu shot."

Since this goes out under the company's name, it's worth having the column checked against your national health agency's flu page, or by an occupational health contact if you have one, before publishing. Your facilities manager may be sincere, but a health tip from the company that's wrong is worse than no tip.
